title: Chapter 68: A Thing Put Back, Part 5 of 5: The Coal Street Pump
html:
The step women were at the Coal Street pump.
They always were, in the early afternoon, when the work of the morning was done and the work of the evening had not begun. Five or six of them, in shawls and clogs and aprons, with their buckets set down on the frozen cobbles round the old iron pump and their arms folded, talking. They were called the step women because they did the steps. The front steps of the big houses and the offices and the banks, every morning, before dawn, on their knees, with a bucket and a brush and a lump of whitening stone. Juno's mother had done steps, before her back went. Half the women in the streets by the river had.
And because they did the steps, they saw everything. Who came out of which door, and when, and with whom. Which carriages stopped where. Which gray coats stood on which corners. They saw it all, on their knees, with their heads down, and nobody ever noticed them seeing it, and then they came to the pump and told each other.
Juno had carried their messages all winter. She knew them all.
Big Maud Croft was there, who did the Chancery steps and was as wide as a door. Win Barrow, thin and sharp, with a voice like a gull. The Pole sisters, Bess and Hattie, who did everything together and finished each other's sentences. And Granny Sedge, who was so old that nobody knew how old, who did the steps of the Bank itself, the great white ones, and had done them every morning for fifty years.
They stopped talking when Juno came round the corner. Then they saw who it was, and started again.
"There she is," said Win Barrow. "Little Juno. Running about on them feet again. Your mother know you're out?"
"She knows," said Juno.
"You've been crying," said Big Maud. Not a question.
Juno did not answer that. She put her hands under the spout of the pump and worked the handle with her elbow and let the water run, so cold it burned, and washed her face in it. When she straightened up, they were all looking at her.
"Something good," said Juno. "At Saint Bride's. I can't say. Something good."
The women looked at each other.
"Well," said Granny Sedge, in her thin cracked voice, from the stone mounting block where she sat with her shawl round her head. "That'll be a change."
And they went back to their talk, the way they always did, as if Juno were not there and also as if she were. She dried her face on her scarf and stood and listened. That was what you did at the pump.
They were talking about the cart.
"Came down Tar Street at the first bell," Bess Pole was saying. "Black as your hat. Same as always."
"Same as always," said Hattie.
"Stopped at the Webbs'."
"At the Webbs'. Again."
"They've only got the one left. The little one."
"The little one."
"And she's gone now," said Bess.
Nobody said anything for a moment. The pump dripped.
"Mother Webb was on the step after," said Win Barrow. "Sitting on her own step. In the cold. With a bag of peppermints in her lap they'd give her. Not eating them. Just holding the bag." Her gull's voice had gone flat. "I said to her, Sal, come in, you'll freeze. And she looked at me like she didn't know who I was. And she said, they said it was for her own good. They said there was a place. Up the hill. Warm. With singing."
"Up the hill?" said Big Maud. "Not out east?"
"Up the hill. That's what she said."
"The house for the simple is out east. Past the tanneries. Where the river bends. Everybody knows that."
"I know where it is, Maud. I'm telling you what Sal said. Up the hill. Singing."
Granny Sedge, on the mounting block, lifted her old head.
"They've painted it," she said.
They all looked at her.
"The cart," said Granny Sedge. "I saw it go by the Bank this morning. Before light, while I was doing the top step. It came up Exchange Street from the river, which it never does, and it went past me close enough to touch, and the lamps were on outside the Bank so I could see." She folded her thin old hands in her shawl. "New paint. White. On the side. Different from before."
"What's it say?" said Win Barrow.
Granny Sedge shook her head slowly. "I can't read, Win. You know I can't. None of us can. It was white letters. A long line. Different from before. That's all I know."
The women were quiet.
And Juno, standing by the pump with her wet face and her scarf in her hands, felt something go cold and tight in her stomach.
None of us can.
She could.
She could, now. A to Z. THE and BACK and PUTTING and CLOTH and BREATHE. She had climbed every wall on a page from the end of the world, this morning, on her own, with the whole crypt listening.
She could read what it said on the side of the cart.
Nobody else at this pump could. Nobody else on these streets, maybe, who would bother to look. The cart had been going up and down the river streets for years with words on its side, and the people whose children it took had never once been able to read what the words said.
"Where does it go after?" said Juno. "After it's been round. Which way?"
The women looked at her.
"East, love," said Big Maud. "Always east. Out along the river. Past the tanneries."
"Not this morning," said Granny Sedge. "This morning it went up Exchange Street. Toward the old town." She looked at Juno with her old pale eyes. "Toward the hill on the other side. Where the black spire is."
Nobody said anything.
Then Win Barrow picked up her bucket, hard, so that the water slopped, and said, "Well, I'm not standing here all day," and the others picked up their buckets too, and the talk was over, the way talk at the pump always ended. Suddenly, and with nobody saying goodbye.
But as Juno turned to go, Granny Sedge put out one thin old hand from her shawl and caught her sleeve.
"It comes back round in the afternoon, Fridays," said the old woman. Very low. "By the fish market. For the ones it missed in the morning. You know that, I expect."
Juno looked at her.
"I know," she said.
Granny Sedge let go of her sleeve.
"Mind your feet," she said. And pulled her shawl over her head, and closed her eyes, and was an old woman asleep on a mounting block, and nothing more.
Juno stood there for a moment by the dripping pump.
Then she turned, not toward home, but the other way. Toward the river, and the fish market, and the Fish Stairs.
The Fish Stairs
She went down to the river the back way.
Through the alley behind the chandler's. Down the slippery wooden stairs by the rope-walk, where Lascar Mary's men were coiling hemp in the cold, their breath steaming. Under the arch of the old customs house. The light was already going gray and thin over the roofs, though it was only the middle of the afternoon. It went early, this time of year. By the fourth bell it would be dusk.
She told herself she was only going to look.
She had the cut-out page folded inside her coat, against her chest, where the packet had been. She could feel it there with every step. And she thought about the two Gideons sitting against the wall in the light of one candle, and the word on the floor between their boots.
GID.
The fish market was nearly empty at this hour. The stalls were bare boards on trestles, wet and scaled and stinking, with the last few gulls walking up and down them looking for scraps. The cobbles were slippery with fish guts and ice. A boy was sluicing down the last stall with a bucket of river water, and the water ran away across the cobbles in a pink stream and down into the gutter and over the edge of the quay into the river. Juno walked round it.
At the far end of the market, where the river wall turned, there were the Fish Stairs.
They went up from the market to the street above. Wide stone steps, very old, worn into hollows in the middle by hundreds of years of fishwives' boots, with an iron rail down one side gone orange with rust. At the top of them there was a street. A narrow one, between the backs of warehouses. And on the street, at the top of the stairs, there was a cart.
Juno stopped at the bottom of the stairs.
She knew that cart.
Everybody did. Everybody who lived near the river, anyway. Everybody who had children, or had been a child, or had known one. It came on Fridays. Every Friday, before dawn, and sometimes again in the late afternoon. It came down from the Hill side of the city and went round the poor streets by the river, slowly, stopping at doors, and then it went away again, east, toward the tanneries and the road where the river bent. Doctor Silas said it went to a house out there. A house with a gold sign on a blue board, for the simple and the aged. He said he had stood at the gate of that house four times and asked for children by name, and been given peppermints, and sent away.
It was black. A closed cart, high and narrow, like a box on wheels, with two gray horses in the shafts and a driver up on the box in a long coat with a plum-colored scarf round his neck. It had a little window on each side, high up, with bars across it. And it smelled. Even from the bottom of the stairs, through the stink of the fish market, Juno could smell it.
Peppermint.
Sweet and sharp and cold. A smell that went up your nose and into the back of your head and stayed there.
The cart was standing at the top of the stairs with its horses' heads down. The driver was sitting on his box, very still, with his hands in his lap, looking at nothing. Waiting. For someone to bring something out of one of the doors.
Juno looked at the side of the cart.
It had always had words on it. Painted in white, in tall neat letters, along the side of the black box. She remembered them from when she was small, before she could read. A long line of white letters that her mother used to pull her away from. And she remembered, too, that this winter, the words had been changing. The step women had said so, on the stairs, at the pumps. Painters, in some yard behind the Ministry, with pots and stencils. And on the door of the cart, the same as always, the round blue seal with the white open hand.
She had never been able to read the old words.
She could read now.
She went up three steps. Then three more. Quietly. On the sides of her feet, in the shadow of the warehouse wall, with her hand on the rusty rail. Until she was close enough to see.
The paint was new. She could see that at once. It shone. White, very bright and fresh against the black, the edges of the letters still sharp from the stencil. And under the new white letters, if you looked, you could still see the old ones. Gray ghosts of letters, painted over in black and showing through, a different shape and a different length.
She read the new ones.
Slowly. Under her breath. Letter by letter, the way the harvester had told her.
THE.
That was easy.
S. P. I. R. E.
She stopped. She knew that word. She had seen it on signs. On the corner of a street up on the other side of the river, where the old town went up the hill toward the great black needle you could see from everywhere.
SPIRE.
The Spire.
And then a stop. A little round dot. And then three more words.
FOR. THE. CHOIR.
THE SPIRE. FOR THE CHOIR.
Juno stood very still on the Fish Stairs with her hand on the rail.
And as she stood there, the driver on the box turned his head. Slowly. Not toward her. Toward the little barred window on the near side of the cart.
There was a face at it.
Small. Pale. A child's face. Pressed up against the bars from inside, with its two small hands round them. A girl, Juno thought, though it was hard to tell. Five years old, perhaps. Six. Thin, with big dark eyes and no expression on her face at all. She was not crying. She was not calling out. She was only looking out, through the bars, at the gray street and the warehouse wall and the top of the Fish Stairs.
At Juno.
She looked straight at Juno, with her big dark eyes and her empty face, through the bars, for a long moment.
Then the driver shook the reins, and the two gray horses lifted their heads, and the black cart moved off down the narrow street between the warehouses, east, toward the tanneries, with its new white letters shining and the old gray ghosts showing through underneath, and the smell of peppermint behind it in the cold air.
The small face stayed at the window until the cart turned the corner.
Then it was gone.
A Little Way
Juno ran.
She did not decide to. Her feet did it, the way they had done it all winter, on roofs and stairs and quays, before her head could tell them not to. Up the last of the Fish Stairs, three at a time, with her hand on the rusty rail, and out into the narrow street between the warehouses, and along it, after the cart.
Her feet hurt. They hurt badly. Every step on the frozen cobbles went up through the soles of her boots and into the bones like a nail. She ran on the sides of them, the way she had learned, and it was clumsy and slow, and she did not stop.
At the corner where the cart had turned, she stopped, and pressed herself flat against the warehouse wall, and looked round.
The cart was a long way down the next street already. Black against the gray. The two gray horses going at a steady walk, heads nodding, the driver still on his box with his plum scarf and his hands in his lap. The street went east from here, along the back of the tanneries, the way the step women said it always went. Toward the bend of the river and the house with the gold sign.
But it did not go east.
At the end of the street, where the tannery wall stopped, it turned left. North. Up the slope toward Exchange Street and the river.
Juno went after it.
She kept to the walls. She kept her head down. She was a skinny girl in a too-big coat with her scarf over her chin, going somewhere, nobody, nothing. She did not run now. Running was what people noticed. She walked fast, on the sides of her aching feet, and kept the black roof of the cart in sight ahead of her, over the heads of the people in the street.
There were more people here. It was the end of the afternoon and the working day was finishing, and men were coming out of the warehouses and the counting houses, and women were coming back from the markets with baskets, and boys were running errands. The cart went through them all at its steady walk. And Juno saw that they moved aside for it. Every one. Without looking at it. The way water moves round a stone. Men stepped back onto the pavement. Women pulled their children in against their skirts. Nobody looked at the little barred windows. Nobody looked at the new white letters. They just stepped aside, and looked at something else, and closed up again behind it as it passed.
Exchange Street. Wide and grand, with the tall gray fronts of the banks and the exchanges on either side, and the Ash lamps along it burning blue in the dusk, whining. The cart went up it. Past the Bank, with its great white steps that Granny Sedge did every morning. Juno saw the steps go by, white and clean and empty. Up toward the top of the street, where it met the river again, at the head of Lantern Bridge.
And there were gray coats on the bridge.
Four of them, this time. Two on each side, at the near end, with their carbines on their backs and their hands behind them. And a wooden barrier across the footway on both sides, painted white, that had not been there yesterday. People were being stopped at it. Asked things. Juno could see a man with a basket being made to open it.
The cart did not stop.
It rolled up to the bridge, and the gray coats on the roadway stepped back from it, the way the people in the street had. One of them lifted his hand to the driver, almost a salute. And the cart went out onto the bridge, onto the long span of it over the gray river, at its steady walk, with its white letters shining in the light of the blue lamps that ran along the parapet.
Toward the other side.
Toward the old town. Where the streets went up the hill on the far bank, steep and crooked, and at the top of the hill, black against the darkening sky, so tall and thin it looked like a crack in the clouds, there was the Spire.
Juno came up to the barrier on the footway.
A gray coat looked down at her. A young one, with a red face from the cold and a thin mustache he was trying to grow.
"Bridge is closed to foot," he said. "Go round by the Old Bridge."
"The cart went over," said Juno.
It came out before she could stop it.
The gray coat looked at her. His eyes went over her. Her too-big coat. Her scarf. Her face. And something in them changed. Got sharper.
"What cart?" he said.
Juno looked at him. At his red face and his thin mustache and his gray cap. At the carbine on his back.
"No cart," she said. "I didn't see any cart."
The gray coat looked at her a moment longer.
"Go round by the Old Bridge," he said again. "Go on. Off home."
Juno went.
She went back down Exchange Street, past the Bank steps, past the blue lamps, with her hands in her pockets and her eyes on the cobbles. She did not look back until she reached the corner. Then she did.
The cart was at the far end of the bridge, very small now. A black dot, with a tiny glint of white along its side. Going up the hill on the other bank. Into the old town. Into the dark.
Up toward the Spire.
She stood on the corner and watched it until she could not see it anymore.
Then she turned round, and went home, the long way, by the Old Bridge, on the sides of her feet, in the dusk, with the smell of peppermint still in the back of her throat, and the small empty face at the barred window still in front of her eyes, and one word going round and round in her head with every aching step.
Spire. Spire. Spire.
Next Friday
It was dark when she got home.
The passage smelled of coal and cats. The purple door was shut, and there was a line of yellow light under it, and when she opened it the forty-one clocks were all ticking, all at once, all slightly out of time, like rain on a roof. The range was lit. The kettle was on. Her mother was at the table with her mending, a shirt that was not theirs, for a lady on Comb Street who paid by the piece.
She looked up when Juno came in.
"There you are," she said. "I was starting to think. Are your feet..."
She stopped. She was looking at Juno's face.
"What's happened?"
Juno did not know how to say it. Any of it. The scratch at the door. The man in the red cap. The two hundred and twelve steps. The page. Reading it slow, all morning, every wall. The gold going in. Gid.
The cart.
She sat down at the table across from her mother. She took off her cap. She unwound her scarf. And she found that she was very tired. More tired than she had been since the fourteen miles.
"Gideon's da said his name," she said.
Her mother put down the shirt.
"Said his... Big Gideon? That hasn't said a word since..."
"He said Gid." Juno looked at her hands on the table. "Just that. Gid. And he looked at him. Like he knew him. And put his hand on his head." She stopped. "That's all. That's all he can do. But he can do that."
Her mother sat very still for a long moment, with her tired face in the lamplight.
Then she got up and came round the table, and put her arms round Juno, from behind, over the back of the chair, and held on. Without saying anything. The way Mrs. Doyle said Lyra had held on to her, in the church, on the night of the fifty-two candles.
Juno let her.
After a while her mother let go, and went to the range, and made tea, and put it in front of her, and sat down again, and picked up the shirt, and did not ask anything more. That was her mother. She knew when to ask and when not to. Juno had never been grateful for it before.
She drank the tea.
Then she got up, and went to the corner by the window where her bed was, and knelt down by it, and pulled the box out from under it. Not the book. The book was under her pillow now. The other box. The little wooden one, that had been her father's, with his tools in it once, and now had her things in it. A whistle on a string, a real Watch whistle, that she had stolen off a sleeping watchman in the autumn and never given back. A button. Two pennies. A blue glass bead she had found in the gutter. And her slate.
It was a small one, the kind they used in dame schools, in a wooden frame, gray and scratched. Her father had bought it for her when she was six, and she had never learned to write anything on it except Juno, and then not even that, until this winter. She took it out, and the stub of slate pencil that went with it, and sat down on the edge of her bed with it on her knees, by the frosty window, where the light from the range just reached.
And she wrote.
She did not have to look anything up. She had the letters in her head. She had looked at them on the Fish Stairs until they were burned into her. White on black, new paint over old.
S.
She made it carefully. A snake. Top round and bottom round.
P.
A line and a belly.
I.
A line.
R.
A line and a belly and a leg. The leg going the right way. She checked.
E.
A line and three arms.
SPIRE.
She sat and looked at it.
The slate pencil squeaked a little, the way it always did. Her mother, at the table, looked up at the sound, and then down again at her mending.
Juno looked at the word for a long time.
She thought about the black cart. The two gray horses. The plum scarf. The peppermint. The old letters showing through under the new ones, gray, like ghosts. She thought about Doctor Silas, standing at the gate of the house with the gold sign four times, being given peppermints and sent away. She thought about the small face at the barred window, with its big dark eyes and nothing in them, looking at her.
At her.
She thought about the harvester's book under her pillow, and the page in it with the heading underlined twice. THOSE I OWE. And her own name on it. SHE CARRIED THE LETTER.
She had carried a letter fourteen miles on frozen feet, because somebody had to.
She looked at the word on the slate.
SPIRE.
The cart came on Fridays. Every Friday. Before dawn, and sometimes again in the afternoon. It went round the poor streets by the river, and then it went east, out toward the tanneries and the road where the river bent. That was what everybody said. That was where it had always gone.
But it did not say that on the side anymore.
It said THE SPIRE.
And nobody, Juno thought, nobody in the whole city, had ever followed it over that bridge and up that hill to see.
She put the slate down on the bed beside her.
Then she took the little wooden barge out of her coat pocket, the one Gideon had made, flat at the front so it could push, with the V cut small into the bottom of it. And she set it on the windowsill, in front of the frost ferns, where the light from the range reached it. It looked very small there. Very brave.
And she took the cut-out page from inside her coat, and unfolded it once more, and looked at the two small lines at the bottom. IT SAYS QUICK. GO QUICK. C. And under them, JUNO. READ IT SLOW. Then she folded it again, along the same crease, and slid it in between the pages of the harvester's book, under her pillow, at the page that said THOSE I OWE. So that it would be with her name.
She sat with her hand flat on the pillow for a moment.
She thought: he owes me. That's what it says.
And she thought: but I don't want him to owe me. I want to be the one who finds out. I want to be the one who reads it. Whatever it says, on the side of the cart, on the door at the top of the hill, wherever it goes. I want to read it slow, and know.
The forty-one clocks ticked round her, all at once, all slightly out of time. The little black one with the painted bird on it said a quarter to midnight.
"Juno?" said her mother, from the table. "What are you writing, love?"
Juno did not answer at once.
Then she put the slate pencil down, and turned the slate round on her knees, so the word faced the room, and the clocks, and the warm range, and her mother's tired face in the lamplight.
"Next Friday," she said. "I'll follow it."
